I am 75 years old and have been working this land in Quzhou County for 55 years. I never went to school, but the fields have been my only teacher. My plot is just 3 mu — small, but it feeds me and my wife. We have a well for irrigation, so when the sky doesn't give us water, I can pump it myself. But diesel for the pump costs money, so I don't waste a drop.

For the winter wheat, I will sow the whole 3 mu after the autumn harvest, once the soil cools down. I buy improved seed from the county supply shop — not the fancy kinds, but the ones my neighbors and I have grown for years because they don't fail. I run the rotary tiller to break up the stubble and make a smooth bed. Wheat needs its food: I spread fertilizer before sowing and then topdress in the spring when the wheat greens up. I will irrigate three times — once right after sowing so the seed catches, once at green-up in March, and once when the heads come out. I don't believe in spraying too much poison. Maybe twice: a herbicide after planting, and a fungicide in spring if the leaves start spotting.

For the summer maize, the race starts the day the wheat comes off in June. Every day lost is a day stolen from the corn. I plant hybrid seed — my father grew the old traditional corn, but these hybrids give much more grain and resist lodging better. I don't till for the maize; I plant straight into the wheat stubble to save time and keep the moisture in the ground. Corn is hungry, especially when it gets knee-high, so I give it a good dose of nitrogen then. Summer usually brings some rain, so two irrigations from the well should be enough if I time them right — one at jointing, one at filling. Two sprays: a herbicide at planting, and insecticide if the corn borers appear, which they usually do.

I have learned not to expect miracles. If the weather holds and I do my part, 450 kg per mu of wheat and 550 kg per mu of maize is what this land gives me. Some years are kinder, some are harder, but I know my field.
